research.title: WebMCP — How Google's New Chrome Protocol Turns Every Website Into a Tool for AI Agents
research.whyTrending: Google shipped WebMCP in Chrome Canary in February 2026. Turns any site into a structured MCP tool. Massive implications for browser agents and dev tooling; almost no practical write-ups yet.

secondaryKeywords: how to make website agent ready
seo.suggestedTitle: WebMCP: Turn Your Website Into a Tool for AI Agents

gaps: Most posts use the deprecated navigator.modelContext and never mention the window.agent -> navigator.modelContext -> document.modelContext (Chrome 150) churn
Shallow 'what is' coverage; few wire a tool to real app logic and show the update-UI-before-return gotcha
Security treated as a footnote; nobody covers tool surface poisoning / Mid-Session Tool Injection or the readOnlyHint/untrustedContentHint annotations
No honest 'should you adopt now' verdict given origin-trial status
Little connection to the wider MCP ecosystem and how WebMCP differs from server MCP and computer-use

apiFacts: Object evolved: window.agent -> navigator.modelContext (deprecated Chrome 150) -> document.modelContext
registerTool(def, {signal}) ; getTools({fromOrigins}) ; executeTool(tool, jsonInputs, {signal}) ; toolchange event
Tool def: name, description, inputSchema (JSON Schema), execute(inputs)->{content:[{type:'text',text}]}, annotations {readOnlyHint, untrustedContentHint}
Declarative attrs on forms: toolname, tooldescription, toolparamtitle, toolparamdescription, toolautosubmit (read-only only)
Unregister via AbortController signal; cross-origin via iframe allow='tools' and exposedTo option; Permissions-Policy 'tools' defaults to self
Availability: Chrome 149 origin trial, chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing, no headless, origin-isolated docs
security: Chrome classifies WebMCP data as strictly untrusted; assumes prompt injection succeeds
Tool Surface Poisoning + Mid-Session Tool Injection (MSTI) via third-party scripts
Defenses: spotlighting, injection classifiers, critic model, human confirmation for destructive ops, server-side validation/CSRF/rate limiting still apply
statistics: Chrome team cites ~89% token savings vs pixel/DOM actuation
W3C Draft Community Group Report published 2026-02-10; Chrome 146 Canary shipped behind flag; origin trial Chrome 149

strategy.angle: Honest, developer-first: WebMCP is real and genuinely clever, but the API is a moving target and the security model is terrifying. Here is what actually works today and whether to adopt.
strategy.title: WebMCP: Turn Your Website Into a Tool for AI Agents
strategy.excerpt: Google's WebMCP lets any website hand AI agents a list of callable tools instead of making them guess where to click. Here's how the API actually works in Chrome today, the moving-target gotchas, and the security model you can't ignore.
hooks: Contrarian: making agents screenshot your UI and guess where to click is the dumbest possible integration API. WebMCP inverts it.
Fact: Chrome cites ~89% token savings vs pixel/DOM actuation.
Gotcha: the API renamed itself three times (window.agent -> navigator.modelContext -> document.modelContext) and most tutorials are already wrong.
outline: Imperative: registerTool wired to real logic
Security: the part nobody wants to read
